title: Simulated canary scenarios lab notes
body:
Purpose:
This doc captures the lab notes from a small simulation exercise run to validate cross-functional canary hypotheses before we bake them into the orchestration UI. Goal was to exercise guardrails (metrics, duration, rollback triggers), cohort selection, and to observe false-positive rates for automated reversion logic under noisy telemetry.

Summary of what we ran:
- Simulation harness: rollout-sim v0.7 (local, dockerized). Synthetic traffic generator replayed a 48-hour production trace sampled from 2024-11, scaled to 10% and 1% traffic slices.
- Variants: baseline (v1.9) vs candidate (v2.0 quantized + batching change).
- Cohorts: global 1% random, geo-weighted 0.5% CA/US, user-activity-strata (heavy/medium/light) split.
- Observability: token-latency, 95th/99th AOI, error-rate (>=500ms error proxy for timeouts), semantic-quality proxy (BLEU-like heuristic from eval harness), cost-per-request estimate.
- Duration: simulated exposures ranged from 15 minutes to 8 hours.

Key findings (high level):
1) Noise floor: for low-traffic cohorts (<=0.5%), the latency signal variance produced a 12% false-positive rollback rate when using a naive 95th-percentile guard. That is, our current trigger is too sensitive for small slices.
2) Cohort stratification helps: splitting by activity tier reduced variance within cohorts — heavy-user cohorts produced stable latency signals and were reliable early indicators for quality regressions.
3) Composite gating worked better: combining a cost-latency composite score with a quality delta reduced false revertions by ~40% compared to single-metric thresholds.
4) Canary warm-up matters: the candidate needed a 20-minute warm-up phase for cache/KV population before meaningful latency comparisons; comparisons before warm-up overstated latency regressions.
5) Rollback chain safety: automated rollback path reliably reverted traffic in the simulation, but human-notification latency (Slack alert -> oncall ack) was the main delay; automation should not assume rapid human intervention.

Experiment matrix (examples we ran):
- Scenario A: 1% global, 15 minutes, metric = p95_latency + error_rate threshold (naive). Result: ~18% false alarms in 24 runs.
- Scenario B: 0.5% geo-slice CA, 1 hour, metric = weighted composite (p95 * 0.6 + semantic-quality-delta * 0.4). Result: stable, <5% false alarms.
- Scenario C: 5% heavy-user cohort, 30 minutes, allow 20 min warm-up. Result: earliest detection of semantic regressions in 7/8 runs.

Operational recommendations (for product + SRE + Observability):
1) Default canary slice: 2% global for first exposure, prefer heavy-user cohort for an immediate small slice where available.
2) Warm-up period: automatic hold for 20m post-deploy before measuring latency/quality signals. Expose metrics with warm-up-aware windows.
3) Composite guardrail: introduce a composite score that combines latency, error-rate, and quality-delta (weights tunable). Trigger thresholds should be percentile-aware and cohort-size aware (see gating rules below).
4) Minimum cohort sizing: avoid automated rollbacks for cohorts with <1000 requests in the measurement window. Instead escalate to human review.
5) Auto-rollback cooldown: after an automated rollback, block auto-redeploys to the same slice for 2 hours and require manual sign-off.
6) Observability hooks: add a synthetic-probe tag that runs light weight quality checks (LLM eval set) within the canary slice every 5 minutes.

Gating logic (sketch):
- measurement_window = max(rolling-10m, warmup-exclusion)
- if requests_in_window < 1000 -> mark as 'insufficient_data' and do not auto-rollback; send P1 alert to owners
- composite = 0.5 * normalized(p95_latency) + 0.3 * normalized(error_rate) + 0.2 * normalized(quality_delta)
- trigger if composite > threshold_by_cohort_size[size_bucket] for two consecutive windows
- size_bucket thresholds (proposal): <1000 -> no auto; 1k-10k -> conservative threshold; >10k -> aggressive threshold

Checklist for running a canary (for oncall / PE):
- Pre-deploy: confirm test dataset and synthetic probes are attached (link to eval harness).
- Start: allocate slice and warm-up timer. Enable tracing (end-to-end) and request sampling at 5% for content QA.
- Monitor: p50/p95/p99 latency, error-rate, quality-proxy, cost estimate. Slack channel: #canary-watch + @oncall.
- Decision gates: after warm-up measure for 2 windows. If pass -> escalate to 5% for broader test. If fail -> auto-rollback or human review per gating.
- Post-mortem: attach telemetry and the sampled request IDs to the incident.

Open questions and follow-ups (action items):
- Q1: How do we pick quality-proxy thresholds for new model architectures? ACTION: Priya will run calibration experiments on 3 representative models by 2025-03-10.
- Q2: Do we want the console to expose composite-score weights with presets (safe/normal/aggressive)? ACTION: Product to propose UI presets (Avery).
- Q3: Where should we surface 'insufficient_data' state in the console? ACTION: Observability to add a visual state and a tooltip explaining the 1000-req rule (Diego).
- Q4: Can we automate warm-up detection rather than fixed 20m? ACTION: Eng infra to prototype cache-priming detection heuristics (Samir).

Notes about simulation limitations (important):
- Replay cannot perfectly model live KV cache behavior or transient downstream slowness; warm-up artifacts are approximate.
- Semantic-quality proxy is brittle for small slices; we used a reduced eval set to speed iterations which increases variance.
- Cost estimates exclude some infra tail effects (GPU spin-up variability).

Appendix: quick config snippets used in the sim harness (for reproducibility)
- traffic profile: sampled_trace_202411.json scaled to 0.01 and 0.1 slices
- canary-config: {"slice_percentage":0.01, "warmup_minutes":20, "window_minutes":5} (see PR in linked_artifacts)

Conclusions:
This lab surfaced several practical gaps in our current rollout defaults: warm-up is under-weighted, small cohorts are too noisy for automated rollback, and a single-metric trigger is brittle. The immediate next step is to prototype composite-based gating in the console with an explicit 'insufficient data' state and to run a second round of sims with richer eval probes.

If you want to reproduce locally: check out GHE PR above, run `./scripts/run_sim.sh --trace sampled_trace_202411.json --slice 0.01 --variant v2.0` and look at `sim-output/*.csv`.

Last updated by Avery Chen (product) — notes taken live in the lab session 2025-02-18 to 2025-02-27.
